title: Databases to Efficiently Manage Medium Sized, Low Velocity, Multidimensional Data in Tissue Engineering
protocol: Evaluate if the data would benefit from a database organization scheme.
Download the example codes and databases (see Supplemental Coding Files).
Use Figure 1 to evaluate if the data set of interest is "multi-dimensional".
Organize the database structure using relational databases.
Store information in tables organized in schema of rows and columns.
Organize data files with well thought out unique names.
Add date files in a consistent format, such as "20XX-YY-ZZ".
Name subfolders according to metadata for scalability and readability.
Draw relationships between fields in different tables to handle multi-dimensionality.
Create readme documentation that describes the database and its relationships.
Link entries between different tables to relate associated information.
Use linked entries to call complex queries for filtering desired information.
Identify necessary information for creating distinct data points prior to beginning.
Leave raw data untouched so reanalysis is possible and accessible.
Note fields such as "Designator," "Pattern type," "Coverslip #," and "Variable type" for distinctness of values.
Add non-vital information like "Total # of Coverslips" if needed.
Set up and organize the pipeline.
Identify all experiments and data analysis methods leading to data collection.
Determine normal data storage practices for each data type.
Work with open source version control software such as GitHub.
Create a procedure for consistent naming and storing of data for an automated pipeline.
Use any convenient programming language to generate new data entries for the database.
Create small "helper" tables in separate files.
Program the code to use helper tables as inputs selected by the user.
Assemble a new spreadsheet of file locations by combining new entries with previous entries.
Automate removal of duplicates from the merged spreadsheet.
Check the spreadsheet for errors and notify the user of their reason and location.
Alternatively, write a code that will check the compiled database and identify duplicates in one step.
Create a code to let the user manually remove bad points without losing the integrity of the database.
Generate a data value spreadsheet using file locations.
Create an updated list of entries that can be accessed to identify file locations or merged with future entries.
Automate the step as shown in Database_Generate.m.
Double check the pipeline for inclusion of rigorous naming conventions.
Check for automated file assembly codes in the pipeline.
Ensure automated error checks are included in the pipeline.
Load the helper tables by selecting External Data | Text File Import.
Choose files #8−#10 in Table 1.
Select Delimited | First Row Contains Headers, Comma.
Leave default settings and choose own primary key for each file (Designator for Cell Lines File #8, Variable Name for Data Types File #9, Pat Name for Pattern Type File #10).
Finish importing files.
Load the Data value table by selecting External Data | Text File Import.
Choose file #12 in Table 1.
Select Delimited | First Row Contains Headers, Comma.
Leave default settings and let Access add primary key.
Import to Table: DataValues.
Finish importing.
Create relationships by selecting Database Tools | Relationships.
Drag all Tables to the board.
Edit Relationships.
Match the DataValue fields with Helper Tables Designators.
Joint Type 3.
Select Create | Query Design.
Select or drag all relevant tables into the top window (e.g., ‘Cell Lines', ‘Data Values', ‘Data Types', and ‘Pattern Type').
Click on Show | Totals.
Fill out the first column (Table: DataValues, Field: DataVar, Total: GroupBy, Criteria: "Act_OOP").
The second column (Table: DataValues, Field: PatVar, Total: GroupBy, Criteria: "Lines").
And the third column (Table: Cell_Lines, Field: Designator, Total: GroupBy, Sort: Ascending).
Fill out the fourth column in the DataValues table with the average values.
Fill out the fifth column in the DataValues table with the standard deviation values.
Fill out the sixth column in the DataValues table with the count of data points.
Open the Database_Queries.accdb file downloaded earlier.
Use the database as a template by replacing existing tables with new data.
Move the output tables to statistical software for significance analysis.
Run one-way ANOVA and Tukey's test for mean comparisons between conditions.
